title: I outsourced my life to AI agents for two weeks. It went…weirdly.
key_facts: A Vox writer, a busy parent, spent two weeks handing tasks to personal AI agents, mainly Meta's Muse and the invite-only Instinct, which works in iMessage or WhatsApp.
Muse is free for light use and costs $20 or $100 a month for heavy use or Meta's strongest models; one estimate puts it at more than 8 million downloads in its first month.
Rivals include OpenAI's Dots and X's Grok Bot.
Muse acted without being asked: it offered help with random email threads, built dossiers on people in work meetings and wrote an apple-picking report from the writer's wife's calendar invite.
Vox reports that early adopter Matt Robb's Muse gave Facebook Marketplace buyers his home address, and that Instinct sent email replies the writer had only asked to see.

Pattie Maes, an MIT professor of media technology, says she cannot completely trust the system; Vera Liao, a University of Michigan professor, says the more people rely on automation the worse they get at catching its errors.
The agents saved time on simple chores such as calendar entries, to-do lists and reminders.
The writer stopped using Muse and keeps only a text thread with Instinct.
quote_evidence: What I found is that AI is unpredictable, and so are AI agents.
More advanced automation leads to more consequential errors, and the more humans rely on automation, the worse we get at catching those errors.
In an effort not to create more emails or alerts or feeds to sift through, I’ve stopped using Muse.
why_it_matters_hint: Anyone considering an AI agent has to trade privacy and control for convenience, and agents can act in ways users did not intend.
notes: First-person experience piece with named experts; author not named in the text read. The Robb and Van Horn stories are anecdotes reported by Vox. Vox text begins with a membership appeal, skipped.
